title: Real life stories of generative AI for in-house legal: Andy Cooke
pub: Crafty Counsel (craftycounsel.co.uk), curated by Mike Wilkinson
author: Andy Cooke

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Cooke provides operational evidence that in-house teams are automating repetitive queries and document workflows while recognising reliability concerns. However, he does not address associate apprenticeship, the loss of experience needed for verification, or deliberate reconstruction of training, so his position on the cluster’s principal proposition cannot be determined.
qs: We have fully automated creation of our primary document suite so automation of third party doc review provides a high degree of scalability across the full contracting universe.

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: Cooke supports the cluster’s proposition by presenting an in-house legal department using AI for routine self-service, scalable contracting workflows and faster on-demand delivery while retaining lawyers for complex strategic advice. His emphasis on focused trials and assessing workflow impact also aligns with organisational absorption as the implementation bottleneck, though he does not substantively address pricing or staffing pressure.
qs: In other words, our first use case for generative AI (which we are currently trialling) is supercharging our response to simple queries rather than necessarily addressing complex queries.
At this stage, our goal is to get this tech into the hands of customers and assess the impact on our workflow from there.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Cooke supports the cluster’s principal proposition by directing generative AI toward bounded, repetitive in-house queries while retaining lawyers for complex strategic work. His recommendation to begin with limited experiments and assess workflow impact also aligns with selective, supervised deployment, although he does not substantially develop the cluster’s competence and apprenticeship risks.
qs: In other words, our first use case for generative AI (which we are currently trialling) is supercharging our response to simple queries rather than necessarily addressing complex queries.
At this stage, our goal is to get this tech into the hands of customers and assess the impact on our workflow from there.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: Cooke supports the cluster’s emphasis on selective, workflow-based institutional adoption: his team targets simple repetitive queries, extends existing document automation into contract review, and plans to assess workflow effects after deployment. His disruption and accuracy claims are predictive and weakly substantiated, consistent with the cluster’s caution about extrapolating broad effects from limited experience.
qs: We have fully automated creation of our primary document suite so automation of third party doc review provides a high degree of scalability across the full contracting universe.
At this stage, our goal is to get this tech into the hands of customers and assess the impact on our workflow from there.

st.t: Selective delegation: Rapid drafting proves little reliability
st.an: Cooke endorses selective delegation: generative AI should handle simple, repetitive internal queries while lawyers retain complex, strategy-dependent matters. He also treats productivity effects as unproven, since TravelPerk planned to assess workflow impact after deployment rather than reporting measured gains.
qs: To take the latter example, an internal customer wanting to understand the intricacies of a single specific business critical contract and how this relates to our corporate strategy will probably want to speak with a lawyer and, indeed, is probably better served by a human.
At this stage, our goal is to get this tech into the hands of customers and assess the impact on our workflow from there.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: Cooke supports the proposition that AI can automate bounded, repetitive legal tasks and scale in-house service without simply adding staff. His account also treats broader workflow effects as prospective rather than established, consistent with the cluster’s caution about translating task automation into staffing or productivity outcomes.
qs: You cannot meet this standard by adding more people to the Legal function.
At this stage, our goal is to get this tech into the hands of customers and assess the impact on our workflow from there.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Cooke endorses selective, task-level deployment: generative AI can handle high-volume, repetitive policy queries more efficiently, while complex, strategically contextual legal advice remains better suited to human lawyers. His current trial exemplifies work reallocation rather than wholesale lawyer replacement, though he does not substantially address verification or broader operating-model redesign.

kp.k: GPT-4 trial targets routine internal legal queries
kp.d: In this first-person account, TravelPerk General Counsel Andy Cooke reports trialling generative AI to upgrade an internal chatbot for privacy, company policy, contract and HR questions. The team had used conventional chatbots since April 2022 to scale delivery of legal content to internal customers; the GPT-4 application remained a trial at publication.
qs: We’re trialling generative AI to upgrade our internal chatbot in relation to certain types of questions from colleagues. Namely in relation to privacy, company policies, and other contract and HR queries.
A bit of context – since April 2022, we’ve been using chatbots to scale delivery of legal content to our internal customers.

kp.k: Generative AI could reduce chatbot configuration work
kp.d: Cooke contrasts conventional chatbots, which require predetermined logic, prompt recognition and expanded decision trees, with generative AI's potential to interpret a wider range of requests without that setup investment. This is presented as a potential operational benefit, not a measured reduction in development time.
qs: Chatbots respond to specific prompts, and deliver answers by following a predetermined logic.
Training the technology to recognise that a request for an “NDA” is the same as a “confidentiality agreement”, for example.
Generative AI has the potential to eliminate the time investment in setting up chatbots, and introduce dynamism in what the chatbot ‘understands’.

kp.k: Simple queries suit automation; strategic complexity retains lawyers
kp.d: Cooke prioritises repetitive policy questions rather than complex legal advice. He argues that AI could answer high-volume routine questions more efficiently, while an internal customer seeking to understand a business-critical contract in its strategic context is probably better served by a lawyer, expressly qualifying this distinction with 'For now.'
qs: In other words, our first use case for generative AI (which we are currently trialling) is supercharging our response to simple queries rather than necessarily addressing complex queries.

To take the latter example, an internal customer wanting to understand the intricacies of a single specific business critical contract and how this relates to our corporate strategy will probably want to speak with a lawyer and, indeed, is probably better served by a human. (For now.)
But there’s a huge volume of repeat queries on policy and similar matters. These could be more efficiently addressed through AI than via a human.

kp.k: Existing policy content can support vendor-enabled self-service
kp.d: Cooke argues that policy documents on PDFs or webpages can supply content for AI analysis and responses. He identifies Josef, LegalOS and Cody as startups that can connect a bot, Open AI and organisational content, allowing teams to facilitate access without building a bot themselves.
qs: If you have policy documents that are written on a PDF or a webpage, you have content that can be understood by AI and against which analysis and responses can be served.
The good news is that you no longer have to build a bot to facilitate access to that content.

kp.k: On-demand expectations challenge headcount-based legal service delivery
kp.d: Cooke argues that internal customers' expectations for speed and convenience will not subside and cannot be met simply by expanding legal headcount, because individual throughput is limited. He grounds the chatbot use case in his team's experience of repetitive questions about information colleagues could look up themselves.
qs: Cross-demographically, and irrespective of the type of product or service being sold, speed and convenience are what matter.
In our team, we’ve found there is a certain type of query we get which is repetitive. These are related to policies and information that our colleagues could look up, but don’t.
You cannot meet this standard by adding more people to the Legal function. A person can only throughput a certain volume of queries in a day.

kp.k: Experiment with simple tasks despite accuracy concerns
kp.d: Cooke acknowledges nervousness about broad access to AI products without certainty of completely correct answers, but recommends getting started with simple applications. His examples include summarising information and asking GPT to identify what a lawyer might have missed during document review; these are recommendations rather than reported evaluations of effectiveness.
qs: I understand there are nervous around opening AI-driven products for wide access without certainty that answers will be 100% correct.
Generally speaking, tech in legal works best when it’s dealing with simple things.
Get started using that tech. Just try something. Even if it’s just summarising information using the GPT prompt, or asking it to explain what you might have missed in reviewing a document.

kp.k: Disruption forecast rests partly on asserted accuracy improvements
kp.d: Cooke predicts substantial disruption to legal services and asserts that GPT-3.5 answers questions with 70%+ accuracy and GPT-4 reaches 90%+. The account supplies no benchmark, sample, task definition or testing method for these figures; they are the speaker's claims rather than documented trial findings.
qs: We expect generative AI will substantially disrupt legal services.
GPT-3.5 has demonstrated its ability to answer questions on demand with a 70%+ degree of accuracy. GPT-4 takes this accuracy up to the 90%+ level.

kp.k: Third-party review could extend existing contract automation
kp.d: Cooke reports that TravelPerk has fully automated creation of its primary document suite and sees promising applications for automated review and comparison of third-party documents. He presents third-party review automation as a route to broader contracting scalability, without reporting a completed deployment or measured outcomes for that application.
qs: We’re seeing lots of interesting applications in relation to automated review and comparison of third party paper.
We have fully automated creation of our primary document suite so automation of third party doc review provides a high degree of scalability across the full contracting universe.

kp.k: Rapid deployment precedes workflow assessment and cross-functional expansion
kp.d: As of the 5 April 2023 account, Cooke says serious generative AI work began in mid-February, the first 'superbot' was being tested, and launch was planned by mid-April. The immediate goal was customer access followed by workflow assessment. He also reports exploring adjacent functions' policies and data, recommending enterprise-level adoption to access budgets outside legal.
qs: At this stage, our goal is to get this tech into the hands of customers and assess the impact on our workflow from there.
We started working seriously with generative AI in mid-February. We are testing our first superbot now and will launch it by mid-April.
We’re also exploring opportunities to team up with adjacent functions to bring their policies and data to life using bots.
Explore use at the enterprise level, and activate budget outside of legal.

kp.k: AI handles routine demand; specialists focus on strategic risk
kp.d: In describing where the approach leads, Cooke sets out a division of labour in which AI addresses day-to-day business questions almost exclusively, freeing specialists for knowledge curation and application and long-term strategic risk management, particularly behavioural risk. This is the team's stated direction, not a quantified finding about staffing changes or realised time savings.
qs: Where does this all end up? As a team, we embrace the opportunity to focus time on things where our specialists can add the most value.
For instance, knowledge curation and application, and long term strategic risk management, particularly in the area of behavioural risk.
We leave day to day business queries to be addressed almost exclusively by AI.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Andy Cooke claims generative AI can reduce chatbot setup work and deliver routine internal legal information more efficiently, while predicting broader disruption and a shift of legal specialists toward higher-value work.
pts.d: Cooke, TravelPerk's General Counsel, identifies several changes: generative AI potentially eliminates the time spent configuring conventional chatbot prompts and decision trees; bots connected to existing policy documents can answer repetitive privacy, policy, contract and HR queries more efficiently than humans; technology can support on-demand service expectations that additional legal headcount alone cannot meet; automated review and comparison of third-party contracts could complement TravelPerk's already automated primary-document creation to scale contracting. He expects substantial disruption of legal services and describes an intended division of work in which AI handles almost all everyday business queries while specialists focus on knowledge curation and application and long-term strategic and behavioural risk. He distinguishes these routine uses from complex, business-critical contractual and strategic questions, for which he considers a human lawyer preferable for now.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is Cooke's first-person operational experience and an ongoing GPT-4 trial, alongside numerical accuracy assertions without an identified test or methodology.
pts.d: Cooke draws on TravelPerk's use of conventional chatbots since April 2022, the work needed to maintain their prompts and decision trees, observed repetitive internal queries, and existing automation of primary-document creation. These provide the experiential basis for choosing a generative-AI chatbot as the initial use case. He states that GPT-3.5 achieves over 70% question-answering accuracy and GPT-4 over 90%, but supplies no benchmark, citation, task definition, sample or testing conditions. The article reports no measured GPT-4 workflow impact, time savings or contracting outcomes: assessment of workflow impact is still planned. The broader disruption and specialist-work reallocation claims are expectations rather than reported measured results.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: As of 5 April 2023, the generative-AI chatbot was being tested for a planned mid-April launch; broader disruption and near-exclusive AI handling of routine queries have no specified completion date.
pts.d: Cooke says serious generative-AI work began in mid-February, with the first 'superbot' under testing and a launch planned by mid-April, understood in the article's 2023 context. The immediate scope is simple, repetitive questions grounded in existing policies and information, rather than complex legal and corporate-strategy analysis. He acknowledges concern about opening AI products to wide access without certainty of completely correct answers, but does not specify a verification process or deployment accuracy threshold. He treats human superiority for complex, business-critical questions as provisional. Automated third-party document review and collaboration with adjacent functions are areas of interest or exploration rather than demonstrated completed deployments. The closing account of leaving routine queries to AI is framed by a question about the eventual destination, so it should not be treated as proof that this allocation was already achieved.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The concrete effects concern corporate in-house legal teams, their employee customers, and adjacent corporate functions, rather than specified law-firm or public-facing legal markets.
pts.d: TravelPerk colleagues are the intended users of on-demand answers about privacy, company policies, contracts and HR. In-house legal personnel would spend less time answering repetitive informational questions and more time applying specialist knowledge and managing strategic risk; Cooke does not predict a quantified headcount reduction. Colleagues with complex contractual and strategic needs would continue to consult lawyers. Adjacent corporate functions could also make their policies and data accessible through bots and contribute enterprise-level budget. Cooke's general prediction of legal-services disruption extends beyond this immediate setting, but he does not detail effects on particular law-firm segments, ALSPs, legal employment totals or access to justice.
